option_description: Controls whether the UEBA/behavioral analytics engine is actively constructing and maintaining statistical baseline models for user, process, and network entity behaviors. When enabled, the system continuously profiles normal activity patterns and scores deviations for anomaly detection.
security_impact: This is a prerequisite boolean in the Rego policy for behavioral_anomaly_detection_accuracy. Without it set to true, no behavioral anomaly detection countermeasure credit is awarded regardless of other settings. It enables detection of insider threats, compromised credentials, and living-off-the-land attacks that evade signature-based tools by identifying deviations from learned normal behavior.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the UEBA or behavioral analytics platform management console. Look under Settings > Analytics Engine > Baseline Configuration or similar. Confirm 'Machine Learning Mode', 'Baseline Profiling', or 'Anomaly Detection Engine' toggle is set to Active/Enabled.
how_to_obtain.navigation: UEBA Console > Settings > Analytics Engine > Baseline Profiling
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Toggle or status indicator showing 'Enabled', 'Active', or 'Learning' state for baseline modeling

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the UEBA platform REST API to retrieve current analytics engine configuration status. Replace <platform_url> and <api_token> with your environment values.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <api_token>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 'https://<platform_url>/api/v1/analytics/config' | jq '.baseline_modeling_enabled, .ml_engine_status'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response containing 'baseline_modeling_enabled: true' and 'ml_engine_status: active'

how_to_obtain.instruction: On self-hosted UEBA platforms (e.g., Splunk UBA, Microsoft Sentinel), inspect the analytics engine configuration file for the baseline modeling parameter.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -iE 'baseline_modeling|ml_mode|anomaly_engine|profiling_enabled' /etc/ueba/analytics.conf /opt/ueba/config/engine.yml 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Parameter line showing 'baseline_modeling=enabled' or 'ml_mode=active'

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the UEBA platform operational logs for baseline modeling activity indicators confirming the engine is actively learning entity profiles.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -i 'baseline\|profiling\|model_update\|learning' /var/log/ueba/engine.log | tail -50
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing periodic baseline model updates, entity profile computations, or learning cycle completions

option_description: Records the measured false positive rate as a percentage of total behavioral anomaly alerts generated over the past 30 days. Calculated as (false positive alerts / total alerts) * 100, this metric reflects the tuning quality and operational precision of the behavioral analytics engine.
security_impact: The Rego policy for behavioral_anomaly_detection_accuracy requires this value to be 10 or below for the countermeasure to be credited. High false positive rates (above 20%) indicate poorly calibrated baselines, causing analyst alert fatigue, missed true positives, and erosion of trust in the detection system. A well-tuned system below 10% ensures analysts focus on real threats.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the SIEM or UEBA dashboard and navigate to the Alert Metrics or Detection Quality report section. Filter to the last 30 days and locate the False Positive Rate or Alert Accuracy KPI widget.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SIEM Dashboard > Reports > Detection Metrics > Alert Accuracy (Last 30 Days)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Percentage value showing false positive rate; acceptable threshold is below 10%

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM or UEBA API for alert disposition statistics over the past 30 days to calculate the false positive rate programmatically.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <api_token>' 'https://<siem_url>/api/v1/alerts/statistics?days=30&fields=total,false_positive' | jq '(.false_positive / .total * 100)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Numeric value between 0 and 100 representing the false positive percentage; target is ≤10

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Splunk-based SIEM deployments, run a SPL query against the notable events index to compute the false positive rate over the last 30 days based on analyst disposition tags.
how_to_obtain.command: splunk search 'index=notable earliest=-30d | stats count as total, count(eval(status="false_positive")) as fp | eval fp_rate=round(fp/total*100,2) | table fp_rate' -auth admin:<password>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Single row result showing fp_rate numeric value; values above 20 indicate tuning is required

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the SOC lead or threat detection engineer to confirm whether a formal false positive tracking process exists and request the most recent monthly detection quality report documenting the measured rate.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written report or dashboard screenshot confirming FP rate measurement methodology and current value for the past 30-day window

option_description: Defines the categories of entities actively profiled and monitored for behavioral anomalies within the UEBA/behavioral analytics platform. Entity types typically include user_accounts, service_accounts, endpoints, network_flows, and cloud_identities, each requiring dedicated telemetry feeds and baseline models.
security_impact: The Rego policy for behavioral_anomaly_detection_accuracy requires either at least 3 distinct entity scopes OR the explicit presence of both 'user_accounts' and 'network_flows' scopes with a low false positive rate. Narrow scope leaves entire attack surfaces unmonitored — for example, excluding service_accounts allows credential-based lateral movement to go undetected, and excluding network_flows misses C2 beaconing and data exfiltration patterns.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the behavioral analytics platform's monitoring scope or entity configuration settings. Review which entity types have active profiling enabled with associated telemetry sources confirmed.
how_to_obtain.navigation: UEBA Console > Configuration > Monitored Entities > Active Scopes
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of entity types with status 'Active' or 'Profiling'; target minimum includes user_accounts, service_accounts, network_flows, endpoints, and cloud_identities

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the entity monitoring configuration via the platform's REST API to enumerate all active entity scope types programmatically.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <api_token>' 'https://<ueba_url>/api/v1/entity-scopes' | jq '[.scopes[] | select(.status=="active") | .entity_type]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array of active entity scope strings such as '["user_accounts","service_accounts","network_flows","endpoints","cloud_identities"]'

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the UEBA platform entity configuration file to identify which entity scope types are declared as enabled.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -A 2 'entity_scope\|monitored_entities\|profiling_scope' /etc/ueba/entity-config.yml /opt/ueba/config/scopes.json 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'enabled\|active\|true'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: YAML or JSON configuration showing entity scope types with enabled: true or status: active

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request documentation from the detection engineering team listing all entity types formally in scope for behavioral baselining, including the telemetry data sources feeding each entity category.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Architecture or configuration document listing at minimum 3 entity scopes with confirmed active telemetry ingestion; gaps such as missing cloud_identities or service_accounts should be flagged

option_description: Measures the percentage of managed endpoints that have an active EDR/telemetry sensor currently enrolled, checking in, and reporting telemetry within the last 24 hours. Calculated as (active sensors / total managed endpoints) * 100.
security_impact: The Rego policy for endpoint_telemetry_coverage requires this value to be 95 or above for the countermeasure to be credited. Gaps in sensor deployment create detection blind spots where threat actors can operate undetected. A 10% deployment gap on a 1,000-endpoint environment means 100 machines are dark to the EDR, providing attackers with staging and persistence opportunities invisible to defenders.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log into the EDR management console (e.g., CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint). Navigate to the Endpoints or Sensor Health dashboard and compare 'Total Managed Endpoints' against 'Active / Online Sensors' in the last 24 hours.
how_to_obtain.navigation: EDR Console > Endpoints > Sensor Health Dashboard > Active vs. Total (Last 24h)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Dashboard metric showing deployment percentage; target is 95% or above with no large offline clusters

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the EDR platform API to retrieve total managed endpoint count versus active sensor count and calculate deployment percentage.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <api_token>' 'https://<edr_url>/api/v1/endpoints?status=active&last_seen_within=24h' | jq '{active: .total_count}'; curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <api_token>' 'https://<edr_url>/api/v1/endpoints' | jq '{total: .total_count}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Two counts allowing calculation of (active/total)*100; result should be ≥95

how_to_obtain.instruction: For CrowdStrike Falcon deployments, use the Falcon CLI or API script to compute sensor deployment percentage against the asset inventory.
how_to_obtain.command:
python3 -c "
import requests, json
token = '<bearer_token>'
headers = {'Authorization': f'Bearer {token}'}
total = requests.get('https://api.crowdstrike.com/devices/queries/devices/v1', headers=headers).json()['meta']['pagination']['total']
active = requests.get('https://api.crowdstrike.com/devices/queries/devices/v1?filter=last_seen:>=-24h', headers=headers).json()['meta']['pagination']['total']
print(f'Deployment: {round(active/total*100,2)}%')
"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Printed percentage value; values below 95% require investigation of unmanaged or offline endpoints

how_to_obtain.instruction: Cross-reference the EDR platform's managed endpoint count against the authoritative CMDB or asset inventory to identify unmanaged endpoints not visible to the EDR platform at all.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Reconciliation report confirming EDR-managed endpoints match CMDB total within acceptable variance; unmanaged endpoints should be documented for remediation

option_description: Enumerates the active telemetry data collection channels enabled on enrolled endpoints through the EDR sensor policy. Channels include process execution events, file system activity, registry modifications, memory scanning, and network connection data, each providing distinct forensic and detection value.
security_impact: The Rego policy for endpoint_telemetry_coverage requires at minimum 'process', 'file', and 'network' channels to be present, OR a total of 5 or more channels to be active. Each missing channel represents a forensic and detection gap: without memory telemetry, fileless malware and in-memory injection attacks go undetected; without registry telemetry, persistence mechanisms and run-key modifications are invisible; without network telemetry, C2 communications cannot be correlated to endpoint activity.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the EDR management console and open the active sensor policy assigned to the endpoint fleet. Navigate to the Telemetry or Data Collection settings tab and enumerate all enabled collection channels.
how_to_obtain.navigation: EDR Console > Policies > [Active Policy Name] > Sensor Configuration > Data Collection Channels
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Checklist of telemetry channels with enabled/disabled state; minimum required: process, file, network, registry, memory

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the active sensor policy configuration via the EDR platform API to enumerate enabled telemetry channels programmatically.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <api_token>' 'https://<edr_url>/api/v1/policies/active' | jq '.telemetry_channels | map(select(.enabled==true)) | [.[].channel_type]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array of active channel type strings such as '["process","file","registry","memory","network"]'

how_to_obtain.instruction: For on-premises EDR deployments or policy export files, inspect the sensor policy configuration file to list enabled telemetry channels.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -iE 'telemetry|channel|process_events|file_events|registry_events|memory_scan|network_events' /etc/edr/sensor-policy.conf /opt/edr/policies/default.json 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'true\|enabled\|1'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration entries confirming process, file, registry, memory, and network channels are all set to enabled or true

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the sensor policy documentation from the EDR platform administrator and verify which telemetry channels are explicitly enabled versus disabled, confirming business justification exists for any disabled channels.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy document or exported configuration listing all 5 core telemetry channels as enabled; any disabled channel requires documented risk acceptance

option_description: Reports the overall fleet-wide health status of the endpoint EDR sensor deployment as assessed by the management platform. Valid states are 'healthy' (sensors communicating and collecting normally), 'degraded' (partial functionality or connectivity issues), 'offline' (sensors not checking in), and 'tampered' (sensor integrity has been compromised or disabled by adversarial action).
security_impact: Both Rego policy conditions for endpoint_telemetry_coverage explicitly require sensor_health_status to equal 'healthy'. A 'degraded' status means telemetry collection is incomplete and detection gaps exist. A 'tampered' status is a critical indicator of active adversary interference — attackers commonly attempt to disable or corrupt EDR sensors as an early step in intrusions. Any non-healthy status invalidates the endpoint coverage countermeasure entirely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the EDR management console's sensor health or fleet overview dashboard. Review the aggregate health status summary and look for sensors in degraded, offline, or tampered states that affect the overall fleet health classification.
how_to_obtain.navigation: EDR Console > Fleet Health > Sensor Status Overview > Health Summary
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Fleet status indicator showing 'Healthy' with zero or near-zero sensors in degraded/offline/tampered states

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the EDR platform API for fleet-wide sensor health metrics to determine the overall status classification and count sensors in each state.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <api_token>' 'https://<edr_url>/api/v1/sensors/health/summary' | jq '{overall_status: .fleet_health_status, tampered: .tampered_count, offline: .offline_count, degraded: .degraded_count, healthy: .healthy_count}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response with overall_status 'healthy' and tampered_count of 0; any tampered sensors require immediate incident response

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Microsoft Defender for Endpoint deployments, use the MDE PowerShell module or MDE API to retrieve sensor health status across the fleet.
how_to_obtain.command: Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'https://api.securitycenter.microsoft.com/api/machines?$filter=healthStatus ne ''Active''' -Headers @{Authorization='Bearer <token>'} -Method GET | ConvertFrom-Json | Select-Object -ExpandProperty value | Group-Object healthStatus | Select-Object Name, Count
how_to_obtain.expected_output: PowerShell output grouping machines by health status; any count in 'Inactive', 'Misconfigured', or 'Tampered' categories requires remediation

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the EDR platform event logs or SIEM alerts for sensor health degradation or tampering events generated in the past 7 days to identify systemic issues affecting fleet health status.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -iE 'sensor_tampered|sensor_offline|health_degraded|agent_disabled|protection_disabled' /var/log/edr/fleet-events.log | tail -100
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No entries indicating tampering or mass degradation; isolated offline events should be investigated for patterns

option_description: Controls whether the EDR/XDR platform's policy-driven automated response engine is globally active, allowing confirmed threat detections to trigger containment actions such as host isolation, process termination, and network quarantine without requiring manual analyst approval.
security_impact: This boolean is a prerequisite condition in all three Rego policy branches for automated_threat_containment. If false, the platform operates in alert-only or manual mode, requiring human intervention for every containment action. This dramatically increases mean time to contain (MTTC), allowing ransomware to propagate, data exfiltration to complete, and lateral movement to succeed during the analyst response window. Automated response is the primary mechanism for reducing dwell time below the hour threshold.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log into the EDR/XDR management console and navigate to the Response Policy or Automated Actions settings. Confirm the global automated response toggle is set to 'Enabled' or 'Active' rather than 'Monitor Only', 'Alert Only', or 'Manual Approval Required'.
how_to_obtain.navigation: EDR/XDR Console > Response Policies > Global Settings > Automated Response Mode
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Toggle or mode selector showing 'Automated' or 'Active' state, not 'Manual' or 'Alert Only'

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the EDR/XDR platform API to retrieve the global response policy configuration and confirm automated response mode is enabled.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <api_token>' 'https://<xdr_url>/api/v1/response-policy/global' | jq '{automated_response_enabled: .automated_response_enabled, response_mode: .response_trigger_mode}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response with automated_response_enabled: true and response_trigger_mode: 'automatic'

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the EDR/XDR response policy configuration file for the automated response enablement parameter on self-hosted deployments.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -iE 'automated_response|response_mode|auto_contain|response_enabled' /etc/xdr/response-policy.conf /opt/edr/config/policy.json 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration entry showing automated_response_enabled=true or response_mode=automatic

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the SOC manager or detection engineering lead to confirm organizational policy permits automated response without manual approval gates, and verify the business decision is documented for compliance purposes.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written policy or runbook confirming automated response is authorized and enabled; environments with manual-only approval processes should document the compensating controls justifying this risk

option_description: Enumerates the specific automated response action types that are configured with active policy triggers in the EDR/XDR platform. Actions include network_quarantine (blocking all network access), process_termination (killing malicious processes), host_isolation (full endpoint network cutoff), and account_disable (disabling compromised user accounts).
security_impact: The Rego policy for automated_threat_containment awards credit if automated_response_enabled is true AND any one of 'network_quarantine', 'host_isolation', or 'process_termination' is present in this array. Each action type provides different containment depth: host_isolation is the most aggressive and prevents all lateral movement; network_quarantine allows management traffic while blocking threat communications; process_termination stops malicious execution without full isolation. Missing all three means no meaningful automated containment capability exists despite the response engine being enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the EDR/XDR platform's response policy configuration and expand the automated actions or response playbook section. Enumerate each action type that has an active trigger rule configured on confirmed detection events.
how_to_obtain.navigation: EDR/XDR Console > Response Policies > [Active Policy] > Automated Actions > Configured Triggers
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of action types with active trigger conditions; minimum recommended: host_isolation or network_quarantine plus process_termination

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the active response policy from the EDR/XDR API and extract all configured automated action types with their trigger states.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <api_token>' 'https://<xdr_url>/api/v1/response-policy/actions' | jq '[.actions[] | select(.status=="active" and .trigger_mode=="automatic") | .action_type]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array of active action type strings such as '["host_isolation","process_termination","network_quarantine","account_disable"]'

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the response policy configuration file to enumerate which automated action types are declared as enabled with automatic triggers.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -B 2 -A 5 'action_type\|response_action' /etc/xdr/response-policy.json 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'host_isolation|network_quarantine|process_termination|account_disable' | grep -i 'true\|active\|enabled\|automatic'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration blocks confirming at minimum host_isolation or network_quarantine and process_termination are active automated actions

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the incident response runbooks and SOC playbooks to confirm which automated response actions have been tested in tabletop exercises or actual incidents, verifying they function as configured in real detection scenarios.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Runbook documentation confirming at least one containment action (host_isolation, network_quarantine, or process_termination) is verified functional through testing; untested actions should not be counted as operationally effective

option_description: Controls the confirmation level required before automated containment actions (network quarantine, host isolation, process termination) are executed without analyst intervention. Options range from fully disabled to fully automatic firing on confirmed detections.
security_impact: The Rego policy for automated_threat_containment requires response_trigger_mode == 'automatic' combined with automated_response_enabled == true to earn containment countermeasure credit. Any value other than 'automatic' means containment actions will not fire autonomously, increasing mean time to contain and allowing lateral movement while waiting for analyst approval. This is a high-criticality attribute because uncontained threats expand rapidly.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In CrowdStrike Falcon, navigate to Configuration > Prevention Policies, select the relevant policy, and inspect the 'Real-Time Response' or 'Automated Response' section for the trigger mode setting. In Microsoft Defender XDR, go to Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Automated Investigation and Remediation and check the automation level per device group.
how_to_obtain.navigation: CrowdStrike: Configuration > Prevention Policies > [Policy] > Automated Response | Defender XDR: Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Auto Investigation
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A mode label such as 'No automated response', 'Semi-automatic', or 'Full automation' indicating the current trigger level.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the CrowdStrike Falcon API for prevention policy settings to extract the automated response trigger configuration programmatically.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>' 'https://api.crowdstrike.com/policy/combined/prevention/v1?filter=platform_name%3A%22Windows%22' | jq '.resources[].settings.classes[] | select(.id=="AutomatedResponse") | .settings'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON object containing 'detection_disposition' or equivalent field with value such as 'DISABLED', 'ALERT_ONLY', 'SEMI_AUTOMATIC', or 'AUTOMATIC'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Microsoft Defender, use the Security Center REST API to retrieve auto-remediation settings per machine group.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>' 'https://api.securitycenter.microsoft.com/api/machineGroups' | jq '.value[] | {name: .name, autoRemediationLevel: .autoRemediationLevel}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Array of machine groups with 'autoRemediationLevel' values: 0 = No automated response, 1 = Semi, 2 = Full.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For on-premises SOAR or open-source EDR deployments (e.g., Velociraptor, Wazuh), inspect the response automation configuration file for the trigger mode parameter.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -Ei 'trigger_mode|response_mode|automation_level|auto_contain' /etc/wazuh/ossec.conf /opt/soar/config/response.yml 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A configuration key-value pair such as 'trigger_mode: automatic' or '<active-response><disabled>no</disabled></active-response>'.

typical_values: disabled (common default; most orgs start here)
alert_only (common in mature orgs with high alert volume concerns)
semi_automatic (prevalent in regulated industries requiring human approval)
automatic (used by high-maturity SOCs with validated detection tuning)

option_description: Indicates whether external threat intelligence feeds (e.g., MISP, VirusTotal, Anomali, ThreatConnect) and/or internal feeds are actively connected to the detection/alerting platform for real-time IOC enrichment during alert generation and triage.
security_impact: The Rego policy for threat_intelligence_integration_depth requires threat_feed_integration_enabled == true as the foundational condition before any threat intelligence countermeasure score is earned. Without active feed integration, IOC matching and reputation scoring cannot function, leaving the detection platform blind to known-bad indicators in real time. This is high-criticality because threat feeds provide immediate, operationalized intelligence on active campaigns.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk SIEM, navigate to Apps > Enterprise Security > Configure > Data Enrichment > Threat Intelligence Sources and verify at least one source shows 'Enabled' status with a recent 'Last Updated' timestamp. In Microsoft Sentinel, go to Threat Intelligence > Data Connectors and confirm connectors such as 'Threat Intelligence – TAXII' or 'Microsoft Threat Intelligence' show 'Connected'.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES: Apps > Enterprise Security > Configure > Threat Intelligence Sources | Sentinel: Threat Intelligence > Data Connectors
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more feed sources listed with status 'Enabled' or 'Connected' and a last-sync timestamp within the expected refresh interval.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Splunk Enterprise Security REST API to list configured threat intelligence sources and their enabled status.

how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON entries where 'disabled' field is false for at least one threat intelligence source.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a MISP-integrated system, verify active feed pull jobs are running and feeds are enabled in MISP's feed configuration.

how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output confirming feed fetch success with event counts, not errors or disabled status messages.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search SIEM ingestion logs or EDR connector logs for recent threat feed sync events to confirm active data flow from intelligence sources.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -i 'threat_feed\|ioc_sync\|feed_update\|intelligence_sync' /var/log/siem/connector.log | tail -50 | grep -i 'success\|updated\|imported'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log lines showing successful feed synchronization events with timestamps within the last 24 hours.

typical_values: false (default; common in immature deployments with no TI program)

option_description: Defines the breadth of indicator-of-compromise types that are actively matched against ingested telemetry. 'none' means no automated IOC matching, 'partial' means 1-2 indicator types (e.g., IP and hash only), and 'full' means 3 or more types (IP, domain, hash, URL, email) are matched.
security_impact: The Rego policy for threat_intelligence_integration_depth awards the countermeasure when ioc_matching_scope is 'full' or 'partial' combined with active feed integration and reputation scoring. 'none' or 'partial' scope leaves detection gaps — for example, matching only IPs misses domain-based C2, phishing URLs, and malicious email senders. Full scope closes these evasion paths and is required for the strongest policy score.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk Enterprise Security, go to Configure > Data Enrichment > Threat Intelligence Management and review which indicator types (IP, Domain, URL, Hash, Email) have active lookup tables with non-zero record counts. In Microsoft Defender XDR, review the Threat Intelligence > IOC page filter options to see which indicator types have active entries.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES: Configure > Threat Intelligence Management > Indicator Types | XDR: Threat Intelligence > IOCs > filter by Type
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of active indicator type categories with record counts, confirming whether 1-2 (partial) or 3+ (full) types are populated and matched.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Count distinct IOC types actively configured in a MISP or OpenCTI instance by querying the attribute type distribution.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H 'Authorization: <MISP_API_KEY>' -H 'Accept: application/json' 'https://<misp>/attributes/describeTypes.json' | jq '[.result.types[] | select(. | test("ip-|domain|url|md5|sha256|email"))] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer count of active IOC type categories; 0 = none, 1-2 = partial, 3+ = full.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the EDR/SIEM platform API to list active threat indicator matching rules and count distinct indicator type categories referenced.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>' 'https://api.securitycenter.microsoft.com/api/indicators' | jq '[.value[].indicatorType] | unique | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count of unique indicator types (e.g., IpAddress, DomainName, FileSha256, Url, Email) with 3 or more indicating 'full' scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the threat intelligence matching configuration file in an open-source SIEM stack to identify which indicator type parsers are enabled.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'enabled:\s*true' /etc/logstash/conf.d/threat_intel_filter.conf | grep -oP '(ip|domain|hash|url|email)' | sort -u | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Count of enabled IOC type keywords; interpret as: 0 = none, 1-2 = partial, 3+ = full.

typical_values: partial (common early-stage deployment; IP and hash matching only)
full (target state; all major indicator types matched in mature TI programs)

option_description: Controls whether alerts are automatically enriched with reputation scores from threat intelligence sources (e.g., VirusTotal scores, Recorded Future risk scores, MISP threat levels) at the moment of detection or triage, without requiring analyst-initiated lookups.
security_impact: The Rego policy for threat_intelligence_integration_depth requires reputation_scoring_active == true alongside active feed integration to earn countermeasure credit. Without automatic reputation enrichment, analysts must manually query external sources for every alert, significantly increasing triage time and creating inconsistency. Automatic scoring enables rapid prioritization of high-confidence malicious indicators and supports the alert_triage_automation countermeasure indirectly by improving alert quality.

true (target state; present in organizations with SOAR playbooks or SIEM enrichment pipelines)

option_description: An array listing the distinct categories of log sources actively sending telemetry to the SIEM or correlation platform. Common categories include 'endpoint', 'network', 'cloud', 'identity_provider', 'email', and 'dns'. This attribute measures the breadth of visibility across the IT environment.
security_impact: The Rego policy for cross_source_log_correlation requires at least 3 source types (or specifically 'identity_provider' and 'endpoint' with at least 2 total) to qualify for the countermeasure. Fewer source types create detection blind spots — for example, missing identity_provider logs prevents detection of credential-based lateral movement, and missing cloud logs hides cloud-native attacks. High source diversity is foundational to multi-hop attack chain reconstruction.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk, navigate to Settings > Data Inputs > Forwarders to view all connected data sources, or use the Search & Reporting app to query the index metadata. In Microsoft Sentinel, go to Settings > Workspace Settings > Data Connectors and filter by 'Connected' status to enumerate active source categories.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Settings > Data Inputs | Sentinel: Settings > Data Connectors > filter 'Connected'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of connected data source categories (e.g., 'Windows Security Events', 'Palo Alto Networks', 'Azure AD', 'Microsoft 365') that can be mapped to source type categories.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk, query the index metadata to extract all distinct sourcetypes and map them to source categories.
how_to_obtain.command: splunk search '| metadata type=sourcetypes index=* | eval source_age_days=round((now()-lastTime)/86400,0) | where source_age_days < 7 | table sourcetype, totalCount, source_age_days | sort -totalCount' -auth admin:<PASS> -uri https://localhost:8089
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Table of active sourcetypes with event counts and recency, allowing mapping to endpoint/network/cloud/identity/email/dns categories.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Microsoft Sentinel Log Analytics workspace for distinct data table names to enumerate log source categories actively ingesting data.
how_to_obtain.command: az monitor log-analytics query -w <WORKSPACE_ID> --analytics-query 'union withsource=TableName * | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | summarize count() by TableName | project TableName | sort by TableName asc' --query '[].TableName' -o tsv
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of active table names (e.g., SecurityEvent, CommonSecurityLog, SigninLogs, AzureActivity, EmailEvents) that map to endpoint, network, cloud, identity_provider, and email source categories.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Elastic SIEM index pattern list to identify active data streams by category using the Fleet API.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u elastic:<PASS> 'https://<elastic>:9200/_cat/indices?v&h=index,docs.count,store.size&s=docs.count:desc' | grep -v '^\.' | grep -E 'logs-|metrics-|winlogbeat|packetbeat|auditbeat|filebeat' | head -30
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of active index patterns with document counts, where prefix names indicate source type (logs-endpoint, logs-network, logs-cloud, etc.).

option_description: Indicates whether ingested logs from disparate sources are processed through a normalization pipeline that maps them to a common schema (e.g., Elastic Common Schema/ECS, Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework/OCSF, or CEF), enabling unified field references across different source types in detection rules and investigations.
security_impact: The Rego policy for cross_source_log_correlation requires log_normalization_enabled == true as a mandatory precondition for the countermeasure to fire. Without normalization, cross-source correlation rules cannot reliably join events because field names and formats differ between vendors (e.g., 'src_ip' vs 'source.ip' vs 'SourceAddress'). Normalization is what makes multi-hop detection chains possible and is directly tied to whether cross-source correlation rules can function.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Elastic Security, navigate to Stack Management > Index Patterns and verify data views use ECS-compliant field mappings. Check if Fleet integration packages (which enforce ECS normalization) are installed under Fleet > Integrations. In Splunk, check the Common Information Model (CIM) add-on under Apps and verify data models are accelerated.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Elastic: Stack Management > Index Patterns > check ECS fields | Splunk: Apps > Splunk CIM > Data Models > verify acceleration
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ECS-mapped field names visible in Elastic index patterns, or Splunk CIM data models showing 'Accelerated' status with compliant sourcetype mappings.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify Elastic pipeline normalization by inspecting active ingest pipelines that perform field mapping/renaming operations.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u elastic:<PASS> 'https://<elastic>:9200/_ingest/pipeline?pretty' | jq 'to_entries[] | {name: .key, processors: [.value.processors[]?.rename, .value.processors[]?.set] | map(select(. != null)) | length} | select(.processors > 0)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of ingest pipelines with rename/set processors active, confirming field normalization is occurring on ingestion.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Logstash pipeline configuration files for field mapping/mutation filters that normalize fields to a common schema.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'mutate\|rename\|ECS\|OCSF\|common_schema' /etc/logstash/conf.d/ | grep -v '^Binary' | head -30
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Logstash mutate/rename filter blocks actively remapping vendor-specific field names to common schema equivalents (e.g., renaming 'src' to '[source][ip]').

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify Splunk CIM normalization by checking whether CIM-compliant tags are applied to sourcetypes and data model searches return results.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u admin:<PASS> 'https://<splunk>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/SA-CIM/datamodel/model?output_mode=json' | jq '.entry[] | {name: .name, acceleration_enabled: .content["acceleration"]["enabled"]}' | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: CIM data model entries where acceleration is enabled, confirming normalization pipeline is active and being used for detections.

typical_values: false (default; common when SIEM is newly deployed with raw log ingestion only)
true (target state; required for effective cross-source correlation; common in mature Elastic/Splunk deployments using ECS or CIM)

option_description: The count of active detection rules or analytics that reference telemetry from two or more distinct log source categories in a single detection logic chain. These are rules that, for example, join endpoint process events with network flow data, or correlate authentication failures from an identity provider with lateral movement indicators from endpoint logs.
security_impact: The Rego policy for cross_source_log_correlation requires cross_source_correlation_rules_count >= 5 (with 3+ source types) or >= 1 (with endpoint and identity_provider sources). Single-source rules cannot detect multi-stage attacks — for example, a rule detecting impossible travel requires both identity provider login events and network geo-data. Rules with count 0 mean the SIEM is operating as a log aggregator only, with no multi-hop attack detection capability. This is high-criticality because advanced persistent threats specifically exploit the gaps between monitoring silos.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk Enterprise Security, search the correlation rule configuration to count rules that reference more than one CIM data model (indicating multi-source logic).
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u admin:<PASS> 'https://<splunk>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite/saved/searches?search=action.correlationsearch.enabled%3D1&count=500&output_mode=json' | jq '[.entry[] | select(.content.search | test("\\|.*\\|.*join|datamodel.*datamodel|tstats.*tstats"))] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer count of correlation rules whose SPL search references multiple data models or uses join/transaction across source types.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Microsoft Sentinel analytics rules and count those referencing multiple table types (e.g., rules with KQL queries joining SecurityEvent with SigninLogs or AzureActivity).
how_to_obtain.command: az sentinel alert-rule list -g <RG> -w <WORKSPACE> --query '[?kind==`Scheduled`].properties.query' -o tsv | grep -cP '\b(join|union)\b.*\b(SecurityEvent|SigninLogs|AzureActivity|CommonSecurityLog|Syslog)\b.*\b(SecurityEvent|SigninLogs|AzureActivity|CommonSecurityLog|Syslog)\b'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer count of Sentinel scheduled analytics rules whose KQL contains join/union operations across multiple table sources.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Elastic Security, navigate to Security > Rules and filter by 'Enabled' rules. Export or browse the rules list and manually count or filter for rules whose 'Index patterns' or 'Custom query' reference more than one distinct index pattern category (e.g., logs-endpoint.* AND logs-network.*).
how_to_obtain.navigation: Elastic Security: Security > Rules > filter Enabled > inspect each rule's index patterns for multi-source references
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count of enabled rules that explicitly reference 2 or more distinct index pattern categories in their detection query.

how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u elastic:<PASS> 'https://<elastic>:5601/api/detection_engine/rules/_find?per_page=500&filter=alert.attributes.enabled:true' -H 'kbn-xsrf: true' | jq '[.data[] | select(.index | length > 1) | select(([.index[] | test("endpoint|network|cloud|identity|email|dns")] | unique | length) > 1)] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer count of active rules with index arrays spanning more than one log source category; compare to Rego thresholds of 1 (minimum) and 5 (recommended).

typical_values: 0 (default; SIEM deployed but no cross-source rules authored)
1-4 (early-stage; some multi-source rules exist but below recommended threshold of 5)
5-25 (meets Rego minimum for full countermeasure; typical in mid-maturity SOCs)
50-200+ (high-maturity environments with curated detection engineering programs)

option_description: Indicates whether a machine learning model is actively running and assigning confidence or risk scores to incoming alerts, enabling automated prioritization of high-confidence detections and deprioritization of likely false positives. The model must be trained and in active (not shadow/passive) mode for this to be true.
security_impact: The Rego policy for alert_triage_automation requires ml_alert_scoring_enabled == true as a precondition for earning the triage automation countermeasure credit. Without ML scoring, analysts face undifferentiated alert queues where critical detections are buried among false positives, directly increasing mean time to respond. ML scoring is the foundational layer that makes automated triage workflows (deduplication, case enrichment, auto-closure) reliable enough to act on. This attribute is high-criticality because alert fatigue is a primary driver of missed detections in high-volume environments.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Defender XDR, navigate to Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Alert Tuning and check if AI/ML-based alert scoring features (e.g., 'Alert Suppression', 'Alert Correlation Score') are enabled. In Splunk UBA, go to Configuration > UBA Settings and verify ML model status shows 'Running' (not 'Training' or 'Disabled').
how_to_obtain.navigation: Defender XDR: Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Alert Tuning | Splunk UBA: Configuration > UBA Settings > Model Status
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ML scoring feature shows 'Enabled' or 'Active' status, and recent alerts in the queue show a confidence_score or risk_score field with non-null numeric values.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect recent alert records via the SIEM/EDR API to verify that ML-generated confidence score fields are populated at alert creation time.

how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u elastic:<PASS> 'https://<elastic>:9200/_ml/anomaly_detectors?pretty' | jq '.jobs[] | {job_id: .job_id, state: .state, created_by: .custom_settings.created_by} | select(.state == "opened")'

true (target state; present in organizations using Splunk UBA, Elastic ML, Microsoft Defender AI, or dedicated UEBA platforms)

option_description: Controls whether the EDR/XDR/SIEM platform automatically groups related alerts into unified cases or incidents through correlation and deduplication logic, reducing noise and consolidating attack chain events into single actionable records.
security_impact: The Rego policy for alert_triage_automation requires alert_deduplication_enabled == true alongside ML scoring and enrichment integrations to activate triage automation countermeasures. Without deduplication, analysts face unbounded alert volume from repeated detections of the same threat event, increasing mean time to triage and masking high-priority incidents beneath noise. This is a hard gate in the policy: no deduplication means triage automation cannot satisfy either condition.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect recent case or incident records in the SOAR or case management platform (e.g., Palo Alto XSOAR, ServiceNow SecOps, or the native XDR console). Each integration appends structured context to reduce manual analyst lookup time.

With zero integrations, triage automation countermeasures cannot be activated regardless of other settings. Richer enrichment (e.g., threat intel + vulnerability data + asset context) directly reduces mean time to triage by providing reputation scores, asset criticality, and CVE context without analyst pivot work.

When disabled, analysts must manually close every benign alert, inflating queue depth and increasing time-to-triage for genuine incidents. Auto-closure with audit logging is critical so that suppressed alerts remain reviewable for tuning validation.

In Splunk ES, review Configure > Incident Management > Suppression Rules for active auto-suppress policies.

option_description: Controls whether the forensic evidence collection pipeline is actively running on enrolled endpoints, capturing process execution trees, memory snapshots, network packet captures, and file change history for use in incident investigation and legal hold scenarios.

Without this enabled, no forensic data pipeline exists, making incident reconstruction impossible and invalidating legal hold compliance. This is the foundational gate for the entire forensic preservation countermeasure — all other forensic attributes are moot if collection is off.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In CrowdStrike Falcon, navigate to Sensor Policy Management and open the active policy assigned to endpoint groups. Verify that 'Forensic Collection' or 'Full Activity Logging' is toggled on. In Carbon Black Response/XDR, check Sensor Groups > Sensor Settings for 'Data Collection' mode set to 'Enabled' or 'Full'. In Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, confirm Live Response and forensic collection capabilities are active under Device Configuration.

how_to_obtain.expected_output: Forensic or full telemetry collection mode shows as 'Enabled' or 'On' for the policy applied to production endpoint groups.
