option_description: Specifies the protection method applied to forensic log storage to prevent unauthorized modification, deletion, or backdating of evidence. Valid modes are: none (no protection), signed (cryptographic hash or signature applied to log records), immutable (storage backend prevents modification after write), or worm (Write Once Read Many hardware/software enforcement).
security_impact: The Rego forensic_evidence_preservation policy explicitly requires tamper_evident_logging_mode to be one of ['signed', 'immutable', 'worm'] — a value of 'none' will fail the policy condition entirely and the forensic preservation countermeasure will not activate even if all other attributes are correctly configured. Tamper-evident logs are essential for legal admissibility of forensic evidence and for detecting insider log manipulation during incident response.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SIEM platform (e.g., Splunk, QRadar, Sentinel), navigate to the storage or data retention configuration and check whether log signing, WORM storage buckets, or immutable storage backends are configured. For AWS-based deployments, verify S3 Object Lock is enabled on the forensic log bucket with Compliance mode. For Azure, check Immutable Blob Storage policies on the Log Analytics workspace storage account.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Settings > Indexes > [forensic index] > Edit > Review archive policy | AWS Console: S3 > [log bucket] > Properties > Object Lock | Azure Portal: Storage Account > Data Management > Immutable Blob Storage
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Storage configuration shows Object Lock: Enabled with Compliance mode (WORM), or Azure Immutable Storage: Locked with a defined retention period. Alternatively, log signing shows cryptographic signing enabled with a key reference.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the cloud storage API to verify WORM or immutable configuration on forensic log buckets. For AWS S3, retrieve the Object Lock configuration. For Azure Blob, check the immutability policy.
how_to_obtain.command:
# AWS: check S3 Object Lock configuration on forensic log bucket
aws s3api get-object-lock-configuration --bucket $FORENSIC_LOG_BUCKET
# Azure: check immutability policy
az storage container immutability-policy show --account-name $STORAGE_ACCOUNT --container-name $CONTAINER_NAME
how_to_obtain.expected_output: AWS returns ObjectLockConfiguration with ObjectLockEnabled: Enabled and Rule.DefaultRetention specifying mode: COMPLIANCE. Azure returns an immutabilityPolicy with state: Locked.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Splunk deployments, inspect the indexes.conf file for the forensic index to verify that coldToFrozenScript points to a WORM-compliant archive and that no deleteIndex or allow_hot_bucket_move options are present. For on-premises syslog pipelines, verify rsyslog or syslog-ng configuration for TLS log signing output.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Splunk: review forensic index configuration
grep -A 20 '\[forensic\]' /opt/splunk/etc/system/local/indexes.conf
# Check for signing configuration
grep -r 'sign\|immutable\|worm' /opt/splunk/etc/system/local/indexes.conf
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Index definition shows frozenTimePeriodInSecs aligned to retention policy, and a coldToFrozenScript referencing a WORM-compliant archive path. No deleteIndex = true present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that cryptographic signatures on log records are present by retrieving a sample log batch and confirming hash values or signature metadata are appended. For signing mode, check that a log integrity verification tool (e.g., AWS CloudTrail log file validation) returns valid results.
how_to_obtain.command:
# AWS CloudTrail: validate log file integrity (signed mode)
aws cloudtrail validate-logs --trail-arn $TRAIL_ARN --start-time $(date -d '24 hours ago' --utc +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) --end-time $(date --utc +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Validation output reports 'No invalid log files found' with a count of valid log files processed, confirming cryptographic integrity of signed log records.

option_description: Specifies the number of days forensic evidence and associated logs are retained in accessible storage for incident reconstruction, legal hold requirements, and compliance audits. Applies to all evidence types collected by the forensic pipeline.
security_impact: The Rego forensic_evidence_preservation policy requires retention_days >= 90 as a minimum threshold. A value below 90 fails the policy condition, preventing the forensic preservation countermeasure from activating. Compliance frameworks (PCI DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2) commonly mandate 90–365 days; legal hold obligations may extend requirements to years. Insufficient retention destroys reconstruction capability for low-and-slow attacks that surface weeks after initial compromise.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the EDR/XDR platform or SIEM, navigate to storage or data management settings and review the retention policy for each forensic data category. In Splunk, check Settings > Indexes and review the frozenTimePeriodInSecs value converted to days. In Microsoft Sentinel, go to Settings > Workspace Settings > Usage and Estimated Costs > Data Retention.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Settings > Indexes > [forensic index] > Review frozenTimePeriodInSecs | Sentinel: Settings > Workspace Settings > Data Retention | CrowdStrike: Falcon Data Replicator configuration > Retention Settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Retention period displayed in days or derivable from seconds value. Target: >= 90 days. Common compliance-aligned values: 180 days, 365 days, 730 days.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Splunk deployments, directly query the index metadata to retrieve the configured retention period and convert to days. For S3-backed log storage, query the lifecycle policy to determine the transition/expiration rule.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Splunk: calculate retention days from frozenTimePeriodInSecs
splunk btool indexes list forensic --debug 2>/dev/null | grep frozenTimePeriodInSecs | awk '{print "Retention days:", $NF/86400}'
# AWS S3: check lifecycle rule expiration
aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket $FORENSIC_LOG_BUCKET | jq '.Rules[] | {id: .ID, expiration_days: .Expiration.Days}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows 'Retention days: 365' or equivalent. S3 lifecycle rule shows Expiration.Days >= 90 for the forensic log prefix.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the SIEM index configuration or log management platform configuration file to read the raw retention setting. Convert any non-day units (seconds, hours) to days for comparison against the 90-day minimum.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Splunk: read retention from indexes.conf
grep -E '(frozenTimePeriodInSecs|maxDataRetentionAge|retention)' /opt/splunk/etc/system/local/indexes.conf
# QRadar: check retention via configuration file
cat /opt/qradar/conf/store_and_forward.conf | grep -i retention
how_to_obtain.expected_output: frozenTimePeriodInSecs value >= 7776000 (90 days) or maxDataRetentionAge >= 90. Example compliant value: frozenTimePeriodInSecs = 31536000 (365 days).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the data retention policy documentation and compare against applicable compliance frameworks. Interview the data management or legal team to confirm that legal hold procedures trigger extended retention beyond the default period when an incident is declared.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written retention policy specifying forensic data retention >= 90 days, with legal hold override procedure extending to >= 365 days or duration of legal proceedings.

option_description: Enumerates the specific forensic artifact categories actively being captured and forwarded by the evidence collection pipeline. Expected categories are: process_execution_tree (parent/child process chains with command-line arguments), memory_snapshot (volatile memory captures for malware analysis), network_packet_capture (full or sampled PCAP for network forensics), and file_change_history (file create/modify/delete audit trail).
security_impact: The Rego forensic_evidence_preservation policy requires all four expected artifact types to be present in covered_evidence_types: process_execution_tree, memory_snapshot, network_packet_capture, and file_change_history. Missing any one type causes the forensic preservation countermeasure to fail. Each type serves a distinct forensic function — process trees reveal lateral movement chains, memory snapshots expose in-memory malware, PCAP supports C2 channel reconstruction, and file change history tracks ransomware or data staging activity.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the EDR platform sensor policy configuration, review which telemetry collection modules are enabled. In CrowdStrike Falcon, check Configuration > Sensor Visibility Exclusions and Data Collection settings to enumerate active artifact types. In Carbon Black XDR, review the Sensor Settings under Data Collection to see which event types are checked. In Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, confirm Advanced Hunting data types available under Security.Microsoft.com > Hunting > Schema.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Falcon: Configuration > Prevention Policies > [Policy] > Data Collection | CB XDR: Endpoints > Sensor Groups > Sensor Settings > Data Collection | MDE: Advanced Hunting > Schema Reference
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Checklist showing all four artifact types enabled: process execution (including command lines), memory (optional dump on detection), network (PCAP or flow), and file system changes. All four should show active collection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the EDR telemetry API or SIEM to verify that recent records exist for each expected artifact type. Confirm timestamps are within the expected collection interval for each category.
how_to_obtain.command:
# CrowdStrike Falcon: query recent events by artifact type
curl -s -G -H 'Authorization: Bearer $CS_TOKEN' 'https://api.crowdstrike.com/fdr/queries/feeds/v1' \
  --data-urlencode 'filter=event_type:["ProcessRollup2","NetworkConnectIP4","FileWritten"]' | jq '.resources'
# Check each type: ProcessRollup2=process_tree, NetworkConnectIP4=network, FileWritten=file_change
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Resources array returns event IDs for ProcessRollup2, NetworkConnectIP4, and FileWritten event types, confirming those artifact channels are active. Memory snapshot availability verified separately via On-Demand Scan API.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search the SIEM for recent records across all four artifact type indexes or sourcetypes. Use a time-bounded query to confirm each type has produced events within the past 24 hours from production endpoints.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Splunk: check coverage across all four forensic artifact types
| tstats count WHERE index=edr_forensics BY sourcetype, _time span=1h \
| search sourcetype IN ("process_execution_tree", "memory_snapshot", "network_packet_capture", "file_change_history") \
| stats count by sourcetype | eval status=if(count>0,"active","missing")
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All four sourcetypes return count > 0 with status: active. Any sourcetype returning status: missing indicates a gap in covered_evidence_types requiring remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the EDR/XDR deployment runbook from the detection engineering team and verify that all four artifact collection modules are explicitly listed as enabled in the production sensor policy baseline. Confirm memory snapshot collection specifies the trigger conditions (e.g., on detection, scheduled, or on-demand).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Runbook or sensor policy baseline document listing all four evidence types with their collection mode, trigger conditions, and the sensor policy name/version in which they are enabled.

option_description: Controls whether the detection platform maintains a change history for detection rules, including version numbers, timestamps, author attribution, and the ability to roll back to previous rule states. This enables change tracking, regression testing, and audit trails for detection content lifecycle management.
security_impact: The Rego detection_rule_tuning_maintainability policy requires rule_versioning_enabled == true in both its conditions — it is the mandatory prerequisite for this countermeasure to activate. Without versioning, detection rule changes are untracked, rollback after a bad rule causes false positive floods is impossible, and audit trails required for change management compliance (SOC 2, NIST CSF) cannot be satisfied. It also enables the feedback loop mechanism that reduces rule decay over time.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SIEM or detection platform, navigate to the detection rules or analytics management section and check for version history, change log, or audit trail features. In Microsoft Sentinel, open Analytics > [rule] and look for 'Version' field and Last Modified timestamp in the rule properties. In Splunk ES, check Security Content Management for rule versioning. In Elastic Security, open Detection Rules and verify the revision field in rule details.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Sentinel: Analytics > [rule] > Edit > Version number visible | Splunk ES: Security Content Management > [rule] > Version History | Elastic Security: Security > Rules > Detection Rules > [rule] > About tab > Revision
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Detection rules display a version number or revision counter (e.g., v3, revision: 5) and a Last Modified timestamp with an associated user or change ticket reference.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the detection platform API to retrieve rule metadata including version information. For Microsoft Sentinel, retrieve analytics rule details and confirm the version property is populated. For Elastic Security, query the detection rules API for the revision field.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Elastic Security: retrieve detection rules with version metadata
curl -s -X GET -H 'kbn-xsrf: true' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -u $ELASTIC_USER:$ELASTIC_PASS \
  'https://$KIBANA_HOST/api/detection_engine/rules/_find?per_page=20' | \
  jq '.data[] | {name: .name, version: .version, revision: .revision, updated_at: .updated_at}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output for each rule shows version >= 1 and revision >= 0, with updated_at timestamps confirming version increments are tracked on rule modifications.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Git-backed detection-as-code pipelines (e.g., Sigma rules in a Git repository, Splunk ES content managed via ESCU), inspect the repository commit history to confirm rule files include version metadata in their YAML headers and that commits are attributed to change tickets or authors.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Git-backed detection rules: check version metadata in Sigma rule files
git -C /opt/detection-rules log --oneline --follow sigma/rules/windows/process_creation/*.yml | head -20
# Check version field in rule YAML
grep -r '^version:' /opt/detection-rules/sigma/rules/ | head -10
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Git log shows commit history with message references to rule names. YAML files contain 'version: X' fields with incrementing values across commits, confirming version tracking is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the detection engineering team to confirm that a change management process exists for detection rules, including peer review, version increment requirements, and rollback procedures. Request evidence of a recent rule rollback or version comparison that was performed in response to a false positive surge.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Detection engineering runbook specifying that all rule changes require version increment, peer review approval, and a documented rollback procedure. Evidence of at least one rollback event in the past 12 months confirms the process is operational.

option_description: Controls the method by which outcomes from closed or resolved incidents are systematically fed back into detection rule tuning processes. Determines whether rule updates triggered by incident outcomes are automated, manually documented through a formal process, performed ad hoc, or absent entirely.
security_impact: The Rego policy for detection_rule_tuning_maintainability requires feedback_loop_mechanism to be either 'automated' or 'manual_documented' (combined with rule versioning and review frequency) for the countermeasure to qualify. Without a structured feedback loop, detection rules suffer decay over time as environment changes accumulate, false positive rates rise unchecked, and tuning decisions are lost. An 'ad_hoc' or 'none' value means the EDR/XDR content library drifts out of alignment with actual threat landscape and environment baseline, directly reducing detection fidelity.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the detection engineering or SOC lead to determine whether a formal process exists for feeding resolved incident data back into rule tuning. Ask specifically whether this triggers automatically from the case management system or requires a scheduled manual review step with documented outcomes.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented description of the process: automated pipeline, a formal runbook/SOP referenced by name, ad hoc analyst discretion, or confirmation that no process exists.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the SIEM or EDR management console's detection content or rule management section. Look for automation settings, case closure triggers, or tuning workflow configurations that reference closed incident feedback. Check if rule update tickets are auto-created on case closure.
how_to_obtain.navigation: EDR Console > Detection Rules > Rule Management Settings > Feedback / Tuning Automation OR SIEM > Cases > Case Closure Actions > Rule Update Triggers
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A toggle or workflow configuration showing automated tuning triggers on case closure, a reference to a documented manual review SOP, or absence of any such setting.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the change history or audit log of the detection rule repository (e.g., Git history if rules are stored as code, or the platform's rule change log) and cross-reference timestamps of rule modifications against closed incident dates to determine whether tuning is systematic or sporadic.
how_to_obtain.command: git log --oneline --since='90 days ago' -- rules/ | head -50
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Consistent commit messages referencing incident IDs or case numbers indicate a documented or automated loop. Random, infrequent commits with no incident references indicate ad hoc or none.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SOAR or case management platform API to check whether closed case webhooks or event triggers are configured to invoke a rule tuning workflow or create a detection engineering ticket automatically.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SOAR_TOKEN' 'https://<soar-host>/api/v1/workflows?trigger_type=case_closed' | jq '.workflows[] | {name, trigger, active}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more active workflows with trigger_type of case_closed or similar, indicating automated feedback. Empty result or manual-only workflows indicate manual_documented or ad_hoc.

option_description: Specifies the maximum number of days permitted between formal scheduled reviews of detection rule effectiveness, false positive rates, and currency. This integer value defines the cadence of the detection content maintenance cycle.
security_impact: The Rego policy for detection_rule_tuning_maintainability requires rule_review_frequency_days to be 90 or fewer (combined with rule versioning and a documented or automated feedback loop) for the countermeasure to qualify. Infrequent reviews allow stale, noisy, or outdated rules to persist, increasing analyst alert fatigue and causing genuine threats to be masked by false positive volume. Organizations with review cycles exceeding 90 days—or no scheduled review at all—accumulate rule debt that compounds detection blind spots over time.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the detection engineering calendar, SOC operational cadence documentation, or scheduled task configuration to identify whether a recurring rule review meeting or automated review task exists, and determine its recurrence interval in days.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A specific recurrence interval (e.g., 30 days, 90 days, 180 days) documented in a runbook, calendar invite, or scheduled task definition. Absence of any scheduled review should be recorded as null.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If detection rules are managed as code (e.g., Sigma rules in a Git repository with CI/CD), check pipeline configuration files for scheduled rule validation or review jobs and extract the cron schedule interval.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -r 'schedule\|cron\|review' .gitlab-ci.yml .github/workflows/ Jenkinsfile 2>/dev/null | head -30
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A cron expression such as '0 0 1 * *' (monthly) or '0 0 */30 * *' (every 30 days) indicating the automated review frequency.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the EDR/XDR or SIEM platform's scheduled reports or rule health dashboard for any configured rule effectiveness review reports. Note the delivery frequency configured for false positive summary or rule performance reports.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SIEM Console > Reports > Scheduled Reports > Detection Rule Effectiveness OR EDR Console > Detection Content > Rule Health Reports > Schedule
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A scheduled report with a defined recurrence (daily, weekly, monthly) targeting rule performance metrics. Absence of any scheduled report indicates the review cadence is manual and likely irregular.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the platform API for scheduled tasks or report schedules related to detection rule review and parse the interval from the response.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN' 'https://<platform-host>/api/v1/scheduled-tasks?category=rule_review' | jq '.tasks[] | {name, interval_days, last_run, next_run}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A JSON object with interval_days populated (e.g., 30, 90) and a recent last_run timestamp. Missing tasks or null interval_days indicates no formal schedule.

option_description: Controls whether a security agent or agentless sensor capable of collecting telemetry from cloud-native workloads—including virtual machines, containers, and serverless functions—is deployed and actively reporting across the cloud environment. A true value indicates enrolled, reporting coverage; false indicates a gap.
security_impact: The Rego policy for cloud_workload_visibility requires cloud_workload_agent_deployed to be true, combined with container runtime monitoring and full detection coverage scope, for the countermeasure to activate. Without agents deployed on cloud workloads, the EDR/XDR platform has no telemetry from those environments, creating complete blind spots for attacks targeting cloud-native infrastructure. This is a high-criticality attribute because attackers increasingly pivot through cloud workloads to avoid on-premises detection controls.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log into the EDR/XDR management console and navigate to the asset inventory or sensor management section. Filter the view to show cloud workload assets (EC2, Azure VM, GCP instances, Lambda, ECS tasks) and verify sensor enrollment status and last check-in time for each asset type.
how_to_obtain.navigation: EDR Console > Assets > Sensor Coverage > Filter: Cloud Workloads OR EDR Console > Deployments > Cloud Sensors > Enrollment Status
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Asset list showing cloud workloads with sensor status 'Active' or 'Enrolled' and recent heartbeat timestamps. Missing cloud assets or 'Not Enrolled' status confirms false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the EDR platform API for enrolled sensors and filter by cloud provider or asset type tags to determine whether cloud workloads have active agent coverage.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $EDR_TOKEN' 'https://<edr-host>/api/v2/devices?filter=platform_name%3A%22Cloud%22' | jq '[.resources[] | {hostname, status, last_seen, platform}] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-zero count of cloud-tagged devices with status 'normal' or 'online' and last_seen within the past 24 hours. Zero results indicates cloud_workload_agent_deployed is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use cloud provider CLI tools to list running compute instances and cross-reference against the EDR agent inventory to identify unprotected cloud workloads.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-instances --query 'Reservations[*].Instances[*].[InstanceId,State.Name,Tags[?Key==`EDR-Agent`].Value]' --output table && az vm list --query '[].{Name:name, AgentStatus:tags.EDRAgent}' -o table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Instances showing EDR-Agent tag value 'installed' or equivalent. Instances missing the tag or showing 'false' indicate unprotected cloud workloads.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review infrastructure-as-code configuration (Terraform, CloudFormation, Ansible) to verify whether the EDR agent installation is included in cloud instance user data, launch templates, or provisioning scripts.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -r 'edr\|falcon\|crowdstrike\|sentinel_one\|cybereason' terraform/ cloudformation/ ansible/ --include='*.tf' --include='*.yaml' --include='*.json' -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: References to EDR agent installation scripts within user_data, launch_template, or provisioning playbooks confirm agent deployment is codified. Absence indicates manual or no deployment.

option_description: Controls whether runtime security monitoring—implemented via syscall interception (e.g., seccomp, auditd) or eBPF-based sensors (e.g., Falco, Cilium, Sysdig)—is active for container workloads to detect anomalous process execution, unexpected network connections, or unauthorized file system modifications at runtime.
security_impact: The Rego policy for cloud_workload_visibility requires container_runtime_monitoring_enabled to be true alongside cloud workload agent deployment and full coverage scope. Container runtime threats—including cryptomining injections, lateral movement via container escape, and malicious image execution—are invisible to host-only or image-scan-only approaches. Runtime monitoring provides the syscall-level telemetry needed to detect these attack patterns after deployment, which static analysis cannot catch. The high criticality reflects the explosive growth of container-borne attack vectors.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether a Falco or eBPF-based runtime sensor is running within the Kubernetes cluster by listing DaemonSet deployments and verifying pod health across all nodes.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get daemonset -A | grep -iE 'falco|sysdig|aqua|lacework|prisma|cilium|tetragon' && kubectl get pods -A | grep -iE 'falco|runtime|sysdig' | awk '{print $1,$2,$4}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DaemonSet entries showing DESIRED == READY counts equal to node count. All pods in Running state confirms runtime monitoring is active across all nodes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the container security platform console (Aqua Security, Prisma Cloud, Sysdig Secure, or equivalent) and navigate to the runtime policy section to verify that runtime enforcement policies are enabled and actively collecting events.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Container Security Console > Runtime Security > Policies > Runtime Protection > Status: Enabled OR Sysdig Secure > Policies > Runtime Policies > Active Policies
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more runtime policies in 'Enforce' or 'Detect' mode with recent event counts populated, confirming active monitoring. Disabled policies or zero event counts indicate monitoring is not functional.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the Falco or eBPF runtime sensor configuration to confirm it is loaded and rules are active. Check the Falco configuration file for enabled status and rule file references.
how_to_obtain.command: sudo cat /etc/falco/falco.yaml | grep -E 'enabled|rules_file|output|syscall_event_drops' && sudo falco --version && sudo systemctl status falco
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Falco service status 'active (running)', enabled: true in config, and at least one rules file path populated. Service stopped or missing confirms monitoring is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the container security platform API to retrieve runtime policy status and confirm active enforcement across the container environment.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $PRISMA_TOKEN' 'https://<prisma-host>/api/v1/policies/runtime/container' | jq '[.[] | select(.effect == "alert" or .effect == "block")] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-zero count of runtime policies in alert or block effect. Zero active policies or empty response confirms container_runtime_monitoring_enabled is false.

option_description: Describes the breadth of cloud workload types actively covered by both telemetry collection and detection rules within the security platform. 'full' means virtual machines, containers, and serverless functions all have active detection policies. 'partial' means only a subset of these workload types is covered. 'none' means cloud workloads are entirely excluded from detection scope.
security_impact: The Rego policy for cloud_workload_visibility requires detection_coverage_scope to equal 'full' for the countermeasure to activate. Partial or absent coverage creates exploitable blind spots—for example, serverless functions are a common target for supply chain injection attacks, and containers are frequently leveraged for cryptomining and lateral movement. A 'partial' value means the platform has structural detection gaps that attackers can identify and exploit. The medium criticality reflects that even partial coverage provides some value, but full parity is required for the countermeasure credit.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the EDR/XDR or CNAPP platform's coverage or asset inventory dashboard and filter assets by workload type. Verify that VMs, container nodes, and serverless functions all appear as monitored assets with active detection policies applied.
how_to_obtain.navigation: EDR Console > Coverage > Cloud Workloads > Filter by Type: VM / Container / Serverless OR CNAPP Console > Asset Inventory > Coverage Gaps > Workload Types
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Full' coverage shows VMs, containers, and serverless all marked as monitored with assigned detection policies. Missing or 'unmonitored' entries for any workload type indicates partial or none.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the security platform API for detection policy assignments grouped by workload type to determine which asset categories have active detection coverage.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN' 'https://<platform-host>/api/v1/detection-policies?scope=cloud' | jq 'group_by(.workload_type) | map({type: .[0].workload_type, count: length, active: map(select(.status=="active")) | length})'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing workload_type entries for 'virtual_machine', 'container', and 'serverless' all with active policy counts greater than zero confirms 'full' scope. Missing any category indicates 'partial' or 'none'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the cloud security or detection engineering team to enumerate which cloud workload types are explicitly in scope for the security platform's detection policies, and request documentation of any formally excluded workload types.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A written or verbal confirmation that VMs, containers, and serverless functions are all covered ('full'), or identification of excluded types indicating 'partial' coverage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use cloud provider CLI to inventory serverless functions and compare against the security platform's monitored asset list to identify coverage gaps for the serverless tier specifically.
how_to_obtain.command: aws lambda list-functions --query 'Functions[*].[FunctionName,Runtime]' --output table | wc -l && curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $EDR_TOKEN' 'https://<edr-host>/api/v1/assets?type=serverless' | jq '.total'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lambda function count from AWS CLI should approximately match the EDR asset count for serverless type. Significant discrepancy (>10% gap) indicates partial or none coverage for serverless workloads.

option_description: Controls whether active, authenticated, bidirectional API connections are established between the EDR/MDR/XDR platform and external security tools such as SIEM, SOAR, ITSM platforms, and identity providers. Bidirectional means both inbound (receiving enrichment or commands) and outbound (sending alerts and events) API communication is functional.
security_impact: The Rego policy for siem_soar_integration_coverage requires bidirectional_api_integrations_enabled to be true as a prerequisite for the countermeasure to qualify, regardless of the number of connected platforms. Without bidirectional API connectivity, coordinated response playbooks cannot execute—the EDR cannot receive enrichment context from identity platforms, and SOAR cannot push containment actions back to the EDR. This breaks the automated response loop that minimizes mean time to contain (MTTC). The high criticality reflects that siloed tools without integration create significant response latency.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the EDR/XDR platform's integration or API management section and review the list of configured connectors. Verify that each listed integration shows bidirectional status (both inbound and outbound arrows or 'send/receive' toggles) and has a recent successful connection test timestamp.
how_to_obtain.navigation: EDR Console > Settings > Integrations > API Connectors > Status: Active AND Splunk SIEM > Settings > Data Inputs > EDR Integration > Verify Bidirectional
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integration entries showing 'Connected', 'Bidirectional', or 'Send & Receive' status with last successful sync within the past 24 hours. 'One-way' or 'Disconnected' status indicates bidirectional is not enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the platform's integration management API to list configured API connections and verify both inbound and outbound capability flags are active.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN' 'https://<edr-host>/api/v1/integrations' | jq '.integrations[] | {name, type, bidirectional, status, last_connected}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integration objects with bidirectional: true and status: 'active' confirm bidirectional connectivity. bidirectional: false or status: 'error'/'disconnected' indicates the attribute is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test bidirectionality by verifying that the SIEM can push enrichment data to the EDR API and the EDR can push alert data to the SIEM API, confirming both directions are authenticated and functional.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SIEM_TOKEN' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"test":true}' 'https://<edr-host>/api/v1/ingest/test' && curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $EDR_TOKEN' 'https://<siem-host>/api/v1/alerts?limit=1'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Both curl commands return HTTP 200 with valid response bodies, confirming both directions of the API connection are functional. HTTP 401, 403, or connection errors indicate the integration is broken or one-directional.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the integration or API gateway logs on both the EDR platform and the connected SIEM/SOAR to confirm bidirectional traffic—look for both inbound API calls from external systems and outbound event pushes to external systems within a recent time window.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'POST|PUT|PATCH' /var/log/edr-platform/api-access.log | grep -v '127.0.0.1' | tail -50 && grep -E 'GET|POST' /var/log/siem/api-gateway.log | grep 'edr' | tail -50
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing recent inbound API calls from SIEM/SOAR IP ranges to the EDR, and outbound calls from the EDR to external platform endpoints, within the last 24 hours.

option_description: An array listing the categories of external security platform actively integrated via authenticated API connections with the EDR/MDR/XDR platform. Common values include SIEM, SOAR, ITSM, and identity providers. Each entry represents a distinct platform category with a verified, active API connection.
security_impact: The Rego policy for siem_soar_integration_coverage has two qualifying conditions: at least two platform types present in this array (combined with bidirectional API and active playbooks), OR specifically both 'SIEM' and 'SOAR' present with active playbooks. Without multiple integrated platform types, automated response orchestration is limited—SIEM provides detection correlation, SOAR provides playbook execution, ITSM provides ticket tracking, and identity integration enables account-level response actions. Missing any of these categories reduces response automation depth and forces manual handoffs between tools.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the EDR/XDR platform's integration management console and enumerate all active API connectors by category. Record each connected platform's type label (SIEM, SOAR, ITSM, Identity, Threat Intelligence) and verify each shows an authenticated, active connection status.
how_to_obtain.navigation: EDR Console > Settings > Integrations > All Integrations > Filter: Status = Active > Group by Category
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A categorized list of active integrations such as: SIEM (Splunk/Sentinel), SOAR (Palo Alto XSOAR/Splunk SOAR), ITSM (ServiceNow/Jira), Identity (Okta/Azure AD). Empty list or only one category present indicates limited integration breadth.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the list of active integrations from the platform API and extract unique platform type categories to build the array of integrated_platform_types.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN' 'https://<edr-host>/api/v1/integrations?status=active' | jq '[.integrations[].platform_type] | unique'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A JSON array such as ["SIEM", "SOAR", "ITSM", "identity"] representing all distinct connected platform categories. An empty array or single-item array indicates insufficient integration coverage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the security architecture diagram or integration map from the SOC or security engineering team. Verify which external platforms have documented, tested API connections to the EDR/XDR and categorize each by function type.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An architecture diagram or integration register listing active connections with platform names and types. Undocumented connections should be treated as unverified.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If the SOAR platform manages integration configurations, inspect the connector configuration files or playbook input configurations to enumerate connected platform types.
how_to_obtain.command: find /opt/soar/config/connectors/ -name '*.yaml' -o -name '*.json' | xargs grep -l 'enabled: true\|"active": true' | xargs grep -h 'platform_type\|connector_type\|type' | sort -u
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of unique platform_type values from active connector configs such as 'siem', 'itsm', 'identity', 'soar'. Missing expected types indicate gaps in integrated_platform_types array.

option_description: Controls whether at least one automated response playbook, ITSM ticket creation workflow, or alert enrichment workflow is active and has been triggered via the configured API integrations. This attribute confirms that integration pipelines are not merely configured but are operationally executing automated actions.
security_impact: The Rego policy for siem_soar_integration_coverage requires automated_playbook_or_ticket_workflow_active to be true in both qualifying conditions (combined with bidirectional API and either two integrated platform types or specifically SIEM+SOAR). A false value means that even if API integrations are technically connected, no automation is firing—alerts require fully manual triage, ticket creation, and response initiation. This directly increases mean time to respond (MTTR) and dwell time. The medium criticality reflects that manual processes can substitute but with significantly degraded response speed and consistency.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the SOAR platform or EDR automation console and navigate to the playbook or workflow execution history. Confirm that at least one automated workflow has a successful execution entry within the past 7 days, and verify the trigger source is an API event (not a manual test execution).
how_to_obtain.navigation: SOAR Console > Playbooks > Execution History > Filter: Trigger=API / Automated > Last 7 Days OR EDR Console > Automation > Playbook Runs > Status: Completed > Sort by Date
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more playbook execution records showing trigger source as 'API', 'Alert', or 'Automated' with a completion timestamp within the past 7 days. Only manual test executions or empty history indicates the attribute is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SOAR platform API for recent playbook execution history, filtering for automatically triggered runs to confirm at least one active automated workflow has fired recently.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SOAR_TOKEN' 'https://<soar-host>/api/v1/playbook-runs?trigger=automatic&limit=10&since=7d' | jq '{total: .total, recent_runs: [.runs[] | {playbook_name, trigger, status, timestamp}]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: total greater than 0 with recent runs showing trigger: 'automatic' or 'api_event' and status: 'completed' or 'success'. Zero total or only manual runs indicates automated_playbook_or_ticket_workflow_active is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the SOAR or ITSM platform's audit or activity logs for automatically created tickets or playbook execution entries triggered by EDR/SIEM alerts within a recent time window.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'auto_created|triggered_by_alert|playbook_executed|api_trigger' /var/log/soar/activity.log | grep -v 'manual\|test' | tail -20 && grep 'EDR\|XDR\|Alert' /var/log/itsm/ticket-creation.log | grep 'automated' | tail -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing automated ticket creation or playbook execution events referencing EDR/alert trigger sources within the past 7 days. Empty results or only test/manual entries indicate the workflow is not active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Ask the SOC manager or detection engineering team to demonstrate a live or recent automated workflow execution, and confirm the last time an automated playbook or ticket was triggered by a real alert (not a test), including the date and playbook name.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Specific playbook name, trigger event, and execution date within the past 30 days from a real alert. Inability to provide this information or reference only manual processes indicates the attribute is false.
